cancer_indication: Breast cancers harboring oncogenic NTRK1/2/3 gene fusions (rare; enriched in secretory breast carcinoma).
moa: Entrectinib is an ATP-competitive inhibitor of TRKA/TRKB/TRKC (NTRK1/2/3) as well as ROS1 and ALK. In NTRK fusion–positive breast cancers, it inhibits the constitutively active TRK fusion kinase, shutting down downstream pro-growth signaling (including RAS–MAPK and PI3K–AKT–mTOR) and promoting cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis. Entrectinib has central nervous system penetrance, supporting activity in brain metastases when present.

REACTOME_SIGNALING_BY_NTRKS.description: Neurotrophin receptor tyrosine kinase signaling mediated by TRKA/TRKB/TRKC, which can activate downstream cascades that promote proliferation and survival.
REACTOME_SIGNALING_BY_NTRKS.interpretation: In breast cancer cases with NTRK fusions, TRK signaling functions as a dominant oncogenic driver and defines a biomarker-selected, targetable dependency.

HALLMARK_KRAS_SIGNALING_UP.description: A gene-expression program reflecting increased RAS pathway output, commonly converging on MAPK/ERK-driven proliferation and survival.
HALLMARK_KRAS_SIGNALING_UP.interpretation: RAS/MAPK output is a key growth axis downstream of TRK and can also represent a compensatory proliferative route in TRK-driven tumors.

HALLMARK_PI3K_AKT_MTOR_SIGNALING.description: A survival and growth signaling program driven by PI3K activation, AKT signaling, and mTOR pathway output.
HALLMARK_PI3K_AKT_MTOR_SIGNALING.interpretation: PI3K–AKT–mTOR signaling is a major downstream survival pathway engaged by TRK fusions and can support continued tumor viability when activated by additional lesions.

REACTOME_SIGNALING_BY_MET.description: HGF/MET receptor signaling that activates downstream proliferative and survival pathways, including MAPK and PI3K signaling modules.
REACTOME_SIGNALING_BY_MET.interpretation: MET signaling represents a clinically relevant alternative RTK axis that can sustain growth in TRK-driven contexts when activated as a bypass route.

HALLMARK_APOPTOSIS.description: A gene-expression program encompassing intrinsic and extrinsic apoptotic machinery and execution pathways.
HALLMARK_APOPTOSIS.interpretation: Apoptotic competence influences whether tumor cells undergo effective cell death when oncogenic survival signaling is inhibited.

HALLMARK_EPITHELIAL_MESENCHYMAL_TRANSITI.description: A transcriptional program associated with loss of epithelial features and acquisition of mesenchymal traits, including increased motility and cellular plasticity.
HALLMARK_EPITHELIAL_MESENCHYMAL_TRANSITI.interpretation: EMT-like states in breast cancer can be linked to broader drug tolerance and signaling rewiring, potentially altering dependence on the original oncogenic driver.

KEGG_ERBB_SIGNALING_PATHWAY.description: Signaling through ERBB family receptors (including HER2/ERBB2 and EGFR) that activates proliferative and survival pathways such as MAPK and PI3K.
KEGG_ERBB_SIGNALING_PATHWAY.interpretation: ERBB pathway activity is a major breast cancer growth axis and can co-exist with, or dominate over, other drivers in rare dual-driver settings.

sensitivity_genes_up_annotations.interpretation: Presence of an NTRK fusion driver (activating TRK signaling dependence) is described as the foremost determinant of sensitivity to TRK inhibition.

NTRK3 fusion signaling (e.g., ETV6–NTRK3) is described as a dominant oncogenic driver in secretory breast carcinoma and underpins sensitivity to TRK inhibition.

A primed apoptotic state is described as facilitating more efficient tumor cell death when survival signaling is removed; high baseline pro-apoptotic factors (including Bax) are presented as a sensitivity-favoring context.

Loss of pro-apoptotic factors (BIM) is discussed in the context of failure to execute apoptosis; conversely, tumors with primed pro-apoptotic machinery (including BIM) are described as more likely to undergo robust cell death after TRK inhibition.

sensitivity_genes_down_annotations.interpretation: Low expression of anti-apoptotic proteins (including BCL-2) is described as a context in which tumor cells may die more readily once oncogenic survival signaling is inhibited.
Low expression of anti-apoptotic proteins (including MCL1) is described as a context in which tumor cells may be more apoptosis-ready after survival signaling is removed.

resistance_genes_up_annotations.interpretation: Acquired KRAS mutation is described as a mechanism that reactivates ERK signaling and bypasses upstream TRK inhibition, leading to resistance.
MET amplification/upregulation is described as an off-target bypass that can reactivate downstream MAPK/PI3K signaling despite TRK inhibition.
Increased HGF is described as a context for MET pathway upregulation, supporting MET-driven bypass signaling.
PIK3CA activating mutation is described as a co-occurring alteration that can sustain PI3K/AKT output and blunt apoptosis despite TRK blockade.
HER2 (ERBB2) amplification/activation is described as a parallel dominant growth axis that can drive proliferation and survival despite TRK inhibition in rare dual-driver scenarios.
Upregulation of other RTKs (including EGFR) is discussed as a plausible bypass route that converges on shared downstream survival/proliferation pathways.
Reactivation of estrogen receptor signaling in ER+ contexts is described as a subtype-linked alternative growth mechanism that can reduce dependence on NTRK-driven signaling.
Upregulation of drug efflux pumps (including ABCB1) is described as a potential pharmacologic resistance mechanism that could reduce intracellular drug exposure.
Upregulation of drug efflux pumps (including ABCG2) is described as a potential pharmacologic resistance mechanism that could reduce intracellular drug exposure.
Upregulation of anti-apoptotic proteins (including BCL-2) is described as a mechanism that suppresses apoptotic execution, allowing persistence despite TRK inhibition.
Upregulation of anti-apoptotic proteins (including MCL1) is described as a mechanism that suppresses apoptotic execution, allowing persistence despite TRK inhibition.
EMT-associated states are described as potentially invoking alternative signaling such as AXL, contributing to drug tolerance and reduced reliance on the original driver.

resistance_genes_down_annotations.interpretation: PTEN loss is discussed as removing a negative regulator of PI3K signaling, enabling persistent AKT pathway output and reduced effectiveness of TRK pathway suppression.
Loss of p53 function is discussed as potentially impairing apoptotic responses and allowing continued survival under drug-induced stress.
Loss of pro-apoptotic factors (BIM) is discussed as limiting apoptotic execution, enabling tumor persistence despite inhibition of upstream oncogenic signaling.
EMT activation is described with E-cadherin decrease; reduced epithelial differentiation markers are presented as part of a drug-tolerant mesenchymal transition phenotype.
Downregulation of negative feedback regulators (e.g., MAPK phosphatases such as DUSP6) is discussed as potentially enabling pathway rebound if suppression is incomplete.

Breast_cancer_subtype_information.HR+/HER2– (Luminal) Subtype: NTRK fusions are extremely rare in luminal breast cancers, but they have been identified. Some ER+ breast cancers acquired NTRK fusions after progressing on hormonal therapy, suggesting a subclone with an NTRK fusion may emerge and drive the tumor. If an ER+ cancer is driven by an NTRK fusion, it will respond to entrectinib, but optimal care might require combined endocrine therapy to suppress any residual ER-driven component.
Breast_cancer_subtype_information.HER2-Positive Subtype: NTRK fusions are similarly uncommon for HER2-positive disease. A reported case described a HER2-enriched breast adenocarcinoma with an ERBB2–NTRK3 fusion and HER2 amplification, implying two drivers. There is no published report of treating such a case with entrectinib; the discussion extrapolates that dual targeting would likely be needed, as entrectinib alone could be insufficient if HER2 signaling remains unchecked.
Breast_cancer_subtype_information.Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC): TNBC is the subtype where NTRK fusions, while still rare, are slightly more encountered aside from secretory carcinoma. True NTRK fusions were described as exceedingly rare in non-secretory TNBC; one TNBC cohort case was reclassified as secretory carcinoma with an NTRK3–ETV6 fusion. Secretory breast carcinoma (often ER/PR/HER2-negative) is defined by ETV6–NTRK3 and has shown very high response rates to TRK inhibitors; scattered non-secretory TNBC case reports with NTRK fusions also support responsiveness. TNBC may have higher likelihood of MET amplification as a resistance mechanism, so vigilance for MET is noted.
Breast_cancer_subtype_information.gBRCA-mutated / HRD+ Subgroup: No known correlation between BRCA1/2 mutations and NTRK fusions is described; they appear independent. If both were present, the text discusses potential dual susceptibilities (PARP inhibitors for BRCA and TRK inhibitor for the fusion), but no reported case is described.
Breast_cancer_subtype_information.Basal-like vs. Other Intrinsic Subtypes: The text notes secretory carcinoma does not fit neatly into typical intrinsic subtypes and that there is not enough data to say intrinsic subtype affects response; the determinant is presence of the targetable NTRK abnormality.

notes: Subtype evidence is limited by the rarity of NTRK-fusion breast cancers; the document emphasizes biomarker-driven use across subtypes. Safety discussion notes no absolute contraindications on label, with strong cautions around embryo-fetal toxicity/pregnancy and key monitoring (e.g., cardiac function, CNS effects, liver enzymes, uric acid, QT).
